source: Pape, Kurtz & Sayama (2015) Complexity measures and concept learning (arXiv v3)
finding: The Shepard Type I-VI difficulty order is not universal. Adults learning separable stimuli (size, shape, shading) show the classic order. A second 'general' order, I < IV < III < V < II < VI, appears with integral stimuli (brightness, hue, saturation), with monkeys, with children, and when difficulty is predicted from identification errors. In the general order Type II is harder than Types III-V.
numbers: General-order sources named: Nosofsky & Palmeri 1996 (integral dimensions), Smith, Minda & Washburn 2004 (monkeys), Minda, Desroches & Church 2008 (children). Classic order: I < II < III,IV,V < VI.
quote: The paradigm-specific order was found to be predictable mathematically by measuring the logical complexity of tasks
limits: Secondary account of the cited experiments; the primary papers were not opened. Which order an LLM should match depends on whether the text stimuli read as separable or integral.
agent_relevance: This reframes gap 1. Claude-v2 finding Type 2 harder than Types 3-5 matches the general order, so it is not clearly an anomaly. Any LLM Shepard test must say which human order it compares against.

source: Pape et al. (2015) quantitative fits of information complexity to Shepard data
finding: A Shannon-entropy 'information complexity' metric fits both human orders. The minimum-uncertainty form fits the classic order; the mean form fits the general order. Feldman's Boolean complexity predicts only the classic order.
numbers: R2 with mean error over 25 blocks: 0.829 (u-min vs Nosofsky et al. 1994 classic data); 0.970 (u-mean vs Nosofsky & Palmeri 1996 general data).
limits: Six types only; authors' own metric, fitted after the fact. Neither entropy level alone recovers the general order; their sum does.
agent_relevance: For gap 6: a complexity signal can predict human difficulty well on small known structures (R2 .83-.97), but which metric works depends on stimulus type. One Boolean-complexity routing score is not safe.

source: Pape et al. (2015) Table 6: rank correlation of complexity metrics with Vigo (2013) human data, 84 structures
finding: On Vigo's separable flask stimuli, information complexity matched or beat Boolean complexity and GIST in rank order for all structure types except 4[2]. Boolean complexity matched human order for 3[2] and 3[3] and was weaker on larger structures.
numbers: Table rows read: 4[3] .986 .926 .986; 4[4] .910 .860 .789 (column headers lost in text extraction).
limits: Column-to-metric mapping uncertain. Human data from one lab (Ohio University undergraduates).
agent_relevance: Boolean complexity is good for small separable problems and loses accuracy on larger ones. Use it as a soft prior only, not as a hard S0 router. Gap 6 stays partly open.

source: Pape et al. (2015) individual differences in Type II
finding: Type II learning looks like a mix of two learner types. Some find a two-dimension rule and learn fast. Others fix on one dimension and learn slowly. Aggregates reflect the mixture.
numbers: No new N; argument rests on earlier published data.
limits: Authors' interpretation, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: A prompted LLM may also mix strategies across samples. Report Type II results as a distribution over runs, not one mean.

source: Rouder & Ratcliff (2004) Comparing categorization models. J Exp Psychol Gen 133:63-82
finding: Four experiments pit rule-based general recognition theory (Ashby & Townsend 1986) against the exemplar generalized context model (Nosofsky 1986). The rule model fit better when stimuli were confusable. The exemplar model fit better when stimuli were few and distinct. Assignment probabilities were manipulated so the two models predicted different things.
numbers: No per-model fit numbers recovered: only the abstract was readable (PMC author manuscript, body not extracted).
quote: stimulus confusion is a determining factor as to which process mediates categorization
limits: Abstract only. Log-likelihoods and N per experiment NOT read. One-dimensional stimuli only.
agent_relevance: Stimulus confusability decides which process runs. For text problems: few, clear, distinct cases invite case-based reasoning; many fuzzy cases invite rule use. Closes the qualitative part of gap 3 only.

source: Smith & Minda (2000) Thirty categorization results in search of a model. JEP:LMC 26:3-27 (search summaries only)
finding: Reanalysis of the 5-4 category structure literature. Search summaries describe 29 or 30 data sets, comparing exemplar and elaborated prototype models. The counts favouring each model were not obtained.
numbers: Summary level only: 29-30 data sets; 193 Scopus citations on the listing page.
limits: Not opened. Do not quote model counts from this line.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for the headline counts. Safe use: 'no model family wins across the classic data sets' is contested, not settled.

source: Nosofsky (2000) comment and Vanpaemel & Pattyn (2006) reanalysis of Smith & Minda 2000 (search summaries only)
finding: Per search summaries, Nosofsky argued that the all-or-none exemplar processes inside Smith & Minda's elaborated prototype models are implausible and lacking in generality. Vanpaemel & Pattyn (2006) reanalysed the same data. Details not read.
limits: Not opened; the PDF fetch returned 404.
agent_relevance: The 'prototype early, exemplar late' story depends on model-flexibility choices. Treat K02 as contested.

source: Goodman, Tenenbaum, Feldman & Griffiths (2008) A rational analysis of rule-based concept learning. Cognitive Science 32:108-154 (not opened)
finding: Rational Rules: Bayesian inference over a grammar of logical rules. Model fits not extracted; the PDF and mirror both failed to open.
limits: Not opened. Two fetch routes returned 404 or a bot wall.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 numeric part stays open. The Bayesian-over-rules idea is already used by K10 (LLM-proposed hypotheses).

source: Liu, Neubig & Andreas (2024) An Incomplete Loop: Deductive, Inductive, and Abductive Reasoning in Language Models (COLM)
finding: Giving the true rule helps a lot when the rule is simple and correct. Few-shot learning and rule induction are dissociated: models can predict well from examples without being able to state the rule.
numbers: Linear functions: GPT-4-turbo 30% few-shot baseline to 96% with the true instruction; GPT-3.5 also improves. Colours domain: true instruction helps all models except Llama-2-7b. Correlation between hypothesis accuracy and ICL success, GPT-3.5 linear: 0.0013 (chance). Four LMs, two problem types.
quote: LMs can sometimes learn effectively from few-shot prompts even when they are unable to explain their own prediction rules
limits: Synthetic arithmetic and nonce-word translation, not category learning. On Kalamang translation most models failed to use the supplied wordlist and grammar sketch.
agent_relevance: Supports 'state the rule' only when the rule is correct. The model's own stated rule can be wrong while its predictions stay right, so rule-then-test needs a real test and not trust in the stated rule. Partly answers gaps 2 and 9.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Kalamang grammar-sketch accuracy
finding: On a real low-resource grammar, the models' self-proposed grammar features were mostly wrong.
numbers: Grammar feature accuracy: GPT-3.5-turbo 27.78%, GPT-4-turbo 22.22%, Llama-2-7B 0%.
agent_relevance: Self-induced rules on messy, non-rule domains are poor. Gate rule-then-test on evidence that the class is rule-structured.

source: Davidson, Gureckis, Lake & Williams (2025/2026) Do different prompting methods yield a common task representation in language models? (arXiv 2505.12075v3; NeurIPS 38)
finding: Instruction-based and demonstration-based prompts use different, partly overlapping model components (function vectors). This is a mechanism study, not a behavioural comparison of rules vs examples on category tasks.
numbers: About 50 simple Todd et al. tasks. Instruction function vectors lift zero-shot accuracy from below 20% to above 50% in the best models. Top 20 heads are about 3% of heads in 3B models vs 2% in 8B. Instruction FVs fail to match demonstration FVs in the shuffled 10-shot setting. Models: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B (base and instruct), OLMo-2.
limits: Small open models only; simple one-step tasks such as country-capital; no frontier models. The behavioural 'rules beat 10-shot in models of 8B or less' claim is only marginal in this paper (reported second-hand by Fu 2026).
agent_relevance: Rules and examples are not interchangeable inside the model. A reason to offer both at S0, but no equal-token effect size. Answers the Davidson half of gap 9.

source: Fu, Cho, Lee & Kim (2026) (arXiv 2609.03213), re-read for the Davidson and Liu claims and the GPT-5.4 reference
finding: Fu says Liu et al. found rules beat examples when the rules are correct, and Davidson et al. briefly reported that rule-based learning of simpler tasks beat 10-shot learning in models of 8B or less. Fu adds GPT-5.4 as a reference: open instruction-tuned models showed similar patterns, but GPT-5.4 is excluded from the mixed-model statistics.
numbers: Open models 7B-32B (Gemma 3, Qwen 2.5, Qwen 3, OLMo 3/3.1) plus GPT-5.4. Adding examples to rules, or scaling examples, gave no consistent significant gain; combined learning tracked rules.
limits: Examples are a minimum-coverage set, so rules vs examples is not token-matched. Rule advantage is largest on Operator Function and Set Game, small or not significant on Tapatan, Noun Class Agreement and Lexical Category Inference, and stronger for disjunctive than conjunctive categories.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: rules beat examples on rule and algebraic tasks, and on the non-rule linguistic tasks the gain shrinks but there is no reported loss. Rule-first looks safe as a default but is not shown to beat examples at equal tokens.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank (arXiv 2509.25140v2): distilled strategies vs raw-trajectory memory
finding: Agent memory made of distilled strategies, including lessons from failures, beat raw-trajectory memory (Synapse) and workflow memory (AWM). Retrieving more items hurt after the first.
numbers: WebArena overall success, Gemini-2.5-flash, 684 tasks: no memory 40.5; Synapse 42.1; AWM 44.1; ReasoningBank 48.8; with test-time scaling 51.8. Gains over no memory: +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 for three backbones. Retrieved experiences (one subset, figure text garbled): 0 gives 39.0; 1 gives 49.7; 2 gives 46.5; 3 gives 45.5; 4 gives 44.4.
limits: Web tasks, not category learning. Extraction method differs between systems, so distillation is confounded with learning from failures.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: distilled (prototype-like) memory beat stored cases at every size tested, and more cases hurt. No crossover where stored cases win was found here.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried & Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (arXiv 2409.07429)
finding: Abstract reusable workflows beat retrieving concrete full examples. Concrete examples bias the agent toward element choices similar to the example.
numbers: Mind2Web cross-task offline step success: Synapse (gpt-3.5) 30.6, AWM (gpt-3.5) 34.6; MindAct (gpt-4) 36.2, AWM (gpt-4) 45.1. AWM vs Synapse: +5.0 element accuracy, +4.0 step success. WebArena gpt-4: rule-induced workflows 35.6 vs LM-induced 35.5.
quote: the abstract, reusable nature of workflows contributes to the superiority of the AWM method
limits: Web navigation. Whole-task success on Mind2Web is very low (2.0 to 4.8).
agent_relevance: Same direction as d13: a distilled routine beats stored cases for repeated task types. Supports prototype-style S0 memory when problem classes recur.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet (arXiv 2504.07952): curated summaries vs full history vs retrieval
finding: A curated, evolving summary memory beat appending full history. Retrieval of similar cases (exemplar style) helped on repeated task types but could confuse the model when suboptimal cases came back.
numbers: AIME 2024: Claude 3.5 Sonnet full history 26.7% vs curated memory 50.0%. GPT-4o baseline 20.0, full history 6.7, DC-RS 40.0. Game of 24: GPT-4o 10% to 99% with retrieval plus synthesis. GPQA-Diamond: Sonnet 59.6 baseline, 63.6 retrieval only, 68.7 DC-RS; GPT-4o 57.1 to 58.1.
limits: AIME has 30 problems per year, so one problem is 3.3 points. 2024-era models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partial: full history (many stored cases) can be worse than no memory; curated summary is better; retrieval plus synthesis is best. Best S0 memory is a summary plus a few retrieved cases.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-Shot In-Context Learning (NeurIPS spotlight; arXiv 2404.11018), Gemini 1.5 Pro
finding: With thousands of examples, in-context classification tracks a nearest-neighbour (exemplar) baseline. Many shots can override pretraining bias, including flipped labels.
numbers: Binary linear classification in 16/32/64 dimensions, 5 random datasets, 25 points per class, 250 test points: up to 2048 shots per class; accuracy rises and approximates k-NN (k=5); slight decrease beyond 512 shots in higher dimensions. 20-digit sequential parity: near-monotone gain to 8192 shots, beating a GPT-2 Medium trained from scratch on 20x more data.
limits: Numeric toy tasks, one model family, no human comparison.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10: when the context holds many cases the model acts like an exemplar learner. This is untested on category structures and runs opposite to the human load finding, where less capacity pushes toward exemplars.

source: Fific, Little & Nosofsky (2010) Logical-rule models of classification response times. Psych Rev 117:309-348 (full text opened)
finding: The paper says rule-based classification models are still proposed and are highly competitive with exemplar and decision-bound models at least in certain paradigms. It cites Feldman 2000 and Goodman et al. 2008 among them. Its own aim is rule models that predict response times.
numbers: The free-drift random-walk comparison model has 14 free parameters (9 stimulus step probabilities plus 5 shared).
limits: Written by exemplar-model authors with designs chosen so rule models can be tested; see K15.
agent_relevance: Confirms the K15 reading that rule-model support is paradigm-bound. No working-memory effect sizes here, so gap 10 stays open.
